title: Traction / EOS in Depth
description: EOS’s full implementation — beyond the overview — repays study because the details decide adoption. The Vision/Traction Organizer’s eight questions (core values, core focus, 10-year target, marketing strategy, 3-year picture, 1-year plan, quarterly rocks, issues list) get answered in two days with the leadership team — the V/TO day. The Accountability Chart (not an org chart — seats defined by 5 roles each, then people matched to seats) exposes the structural gaps. The People Analyzer (values plus GWC per person per seat — the right-people-right-seats tool) makes personnel decisions objective. The Scorecard’s 5–15 weekly numbers get owners. The Level 10 Meeting runs the IDS. The implementation path: the 90-minute meeting pulse taught first, then V/TO, then the tools — or the full two-day with a certified implementer. The data: EOS Worldwide reports hundreds of thousands of companies; the implementer community numbers in the hundreds. The criticism: simplicity that can feel simplistic to complex enterprises — EOS knows its lane (10–250 people) and stays in it.
key_points: V/TO: eight questions in two days
Accountability Chart: seats before people
People Analyzer: values plus GWC objectivity
Lane discipline: 10–250 people
how_it_works: V/TO day, accountability chart, people analyzer, scorecard, Level 10 pulse, quarterly rocks.

title: The Rockefeller Habits Checklist
description: The Rockefeller Habits — Harnish’s original ten, the checklist behind Scaling Up — deserve the full enumeration because the checklist is the product. 1) The executive team is healthy and aligned. 2) Everyone is aligned with the #1 thing that needs to be accomplished this quarter. 3) Communication rhythm is established and information moves through the organization accurately. 4) Every facet of the organization has a person assigned with accountability for ensuring goals are met. 5) Ongoing employee input is collected to identify obstacles and opportunities. 6) Reporting and analysis of customer feedback data is as frequent and accurate as financial data. 7) Core values and purpose are alive in the organization. 8) Employees can articulate the key components of strategy accurately. 9) All employees can answer whether they had a good day or week (the KPI clarity). 10) The company’s plans and performance are visible to everyone. The power: the checklist audits the growth company’s fundamentals in an afternoon. The use: score each 1–10, fix the lowest — the operating system’s health check.
key_points: Ten habits: alignment to visibility
The checklist audits fundamentals in an afternoon
Score 1–10; fix the lowest
The health check for growth companies
how_it_works: Score the ten habits, address the lowest, re-score quarterly, build the disciplines behind each.

title: The Balanced Scorecard in Depth
description: The scorecard’s full method — beyond the four perspectives — includes the strategy map’s cause-effect logic and the implementation sequence. The build: clarify the vision and strategy, define objectives per perspective (the 15–20 strategic objectives), map the cause-effect links (learning objectives enable process objectives enable customer objectives enable financial — the map’s arrows are hypotheses), select measures (1–2 per objective — the discipline), set targets (the stretch that requires the strategy), and align initiatives (fund only what moves the map — the initiative filter). The strategy map’s themes often organize as operational excellence, customer intimacy, product leadership — the value disciplines. The review: the strategy management office runs the monthly review — the map on the wall, the measures discussed, the hypotheses tested. The evolution: Kaplan and Norton’s later work added strategy maps for nonprofits and the “execution premium” (the office that manages the cycle). The failure remains measure bloat — the 40-KPI scorecard nobody reads.
key_points: Strategy maps: cause-effect hypotheses across perspectives
Initiative filter: fund only what moves the map
Monthly review with the map on the wall
Measure bloat is the perennial failure
core_principles: Review the strategy, not just numbers
how_it_works: Map objectives, link causally, measure sparsely, target boldly, fund initiatives to the map, review monthly.

title: Hoshin Kanri in Depth
description: Hoshin kanri’s full practice — the FAIR cycle (Focus, Alignment, Integration, Review) — operationalizes breakthrough strategy. Focus: the 3–5 hoshins selected (the vital few breakthroughs — chosen by the top team from the long-term vision and the current reality). Alignment: catchball deployment — each level negotiates its contribution targets and means with the level above, documented in the X-matrix (south: strategies, west: tactics/improvements, north: results/metrics, east: owners — the one-page deployment). Integration: the hoshins enter daily management — the PDCA cycles, the visual boards, the monthly reviews where red items get help. Review: the annual diagnosis — the president’s audit of the hoshin system itself (hansei — the reflective improvement of the management system). The power: the entire company’s energy focused on the breakthroughs, with the daily work integrated — strategy and operations unified. The demand: the discipline is total — partial hoshin is just goals with Japanese names.
key_points: FAIR: Focus, Alignment, Integration, Review
Catchball deployment via X-matrix
Hoshins integrated into daily management
Annual hansei improves the system itself
how_it_works: Focus the hoshins, catchball down, integrate into daily PDCA, review and hansei yearly.

title: OKR Implementation in Depth
description: OKR practice beyond the basics — the disciplines that separate working OKRs from theater. The cadence: annual company OKRs (the directional few), quarterly company and team OKRs (the execution set — drafted bottom-up, aligned top-down), weekly check-ins (confidence levels and blockers — the 15-minute review), quarterly scoring and retro (0.0–1.0 per key result; the 0.6–0.7 target zone). The drafting discipline: teams draft, leaders align — the 50/50 split (half the team’s OKRs set by the team, half aligned to company) preserves ownership. The key-result discipline: outcomes with baselines and targets (from X to Y by when), 3–5 per objective, the “would we celebrate hitting it?” test. The grading discipline: scores inform learning, never compensation — the moment OKRs touch bonuses, stretch dies. The common pathologies and cures: too many OKRs (cap at 5 per team), cascading as dictation (align, don’t dictate), set-and-forget (the weekly check-in is the system). The tooling: simple docs beat OKR software until scale demands it.
key_points: Annual directional; quarterly execution; weekly check-ins
50/50 drafting: team-owned plus company-aligned
Scores inform learning, never compensation
Cap at 5 per team; align don’t dictate
how_it_works: Draft quarterly, check weekly, score and retro quarterly, keep compensation separate.

title: The McKinsey 7S Model
description: The 7S model (Waterman, Peters, Phillips — In Search of Excellence, 1982) maps organizational effectiveness across seven interdependent elements: the hard three (strategy, structure, systems) and the soft four (shared values, style, staff, skills). The model’s insight: effectiveness comes from the fit among all seven — the structure change that ignores style and skills fails, as every reorganization veteran knows. The diagnostic use: assess each S’s current state, define the desired state, and find the misalignments — the gaps are the transformation agenda. The shared-values center placement matters: values at the core influence all six others — the model’s answer to “culture eats strategy.” The model’s age is its strength and weakness: the elements are timeless, but the model predates networks, platforms, and AI — modern users add the ecosystem and technology dimensions. The enduring use: the pre-transformation alignment check — the seven lenses that catch what the org-chart-only view misses.
key_points: Hard three plus soft four; shared values at center
Effectiveness from fit among all seven
Diagnostic: assess, define desired, find misalignments
Pre-transformation alignment check
how_it_works: Assess the seven, define desired states, close misalignments, recheck after changes.

title: Porter’s Five Forces and Generic Strategies
description: Porter’s frameworks — the strategist’s operating system for market analysis. The Five Forces (1980): industry attractiveness determined by rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power — the structural analysis that precedes strategy. The Generic Strategies: cost leadership, differentiation, or focus — with the “stuck in the middle” warning (the firm that is neither cheapest nor most distinctive). The Value Chain: the firm’s activities analyzed for cost and differentiation advantage — the operational anatomy of strategy. The later work: the Five Forces adapted for digital (platform dynamics, network effects as a sixth force in practice), and the shared-value evolution (strategy serving society as advantage, not charity). The operating use: the annual strategy review runs the forces on each market, positions on the generic strategies honestly, and traces the value chain for the advantage’s sources. The critique: static industry analysis in dynamic markets — answered by using Porter for structure and adding dynamic capabilities for change. The frameworks endure because structure still shapes profitability.
key_points: Five Forces: structural industry analysis
Generic strategies: cost, differentiation, focus — avoid the middle
Value chain: operational anatomy of advantage
Static analysis plus dynamic capabilities
how_it_works: Analyze forces per market, position honestly, trace the value chain, build dynamic capabilities.
t: Porter’s Five Forces and Generic Strategies

title: Blue Ocean Strategy
description: Blue Ocean Strategy (Kim and Mauborgne, 2005) — the framework for creating uncontested market space: instead of competing in bloody “red oceans,” create “blue oceans” of new demand. The tools: the strategy canvas (the industry’s competing factors mapped — the as-is picture), the four actions framework (eliminate, reduce, raise, create — the ERR C grid reconstructing buyer value), the six paths (look across alternatives, strategic groups, buyer chains, complements, functional-emotional appeal, time), and the three tiers of noncustomers (the demand beyond the industry’s edge). The cases: Cirque du Soleil (theater plus circus minus animals and stars), Yellow Tail (wine minus snobbery), Nintendo Wii (gaming plus motion, minus hardcore specs). The execution: the blue ocean must be a system — value innovation (differentiation plus low cost simultaneously) requires aligning the whole business model. The critique: blue oceans turn red (imitators follow) — the framework’s answer is continuous value innovation. The use: the strategy offsite’s creative engine.
key_points: Create uncontested space; don’t just compete
ERRC: eliminate, reduce, raise, create
Six paths to new demand; three tiers of noncustomers
Value innovation: differentiation plus low cost
how_it_works: Canvas the industry, apply ERRC, explore the six paths, build the blue-ocean business model, keep innovating.

title: The Lean Canvas and Business Model Canvas
description: The Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder, 2008) and its startup variant the Lean Canvas (Ash Maurya) compress the business model onto one page: nine blocks (customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships, cost structure) — the whole business visible at once. The Lean Canvas adapts for startups: problem, solution, key metrics, unfair advantage replacing the corporate blocks. The use: the founding document (the first canvas before the first line of code), the pivot record (canvases versioned per iteration — the business model’s git history), and the communication tool (the investor, partner, and team alignment page). The disciplines: fill with hypotheses, not facts (the canvas’s boxes are assumptions until tested — the customer interviews validate them), keep it to one page (the constraint forces clarity), and update it (the stale canvas is the plan nobody follows). The critique: the canvas describes the model, not the strategy — pair it with positioning frameworks. The power: the business model as a discussable artifact.
key_points: Nine blocks: the whole model on one page
Lean Canvas: problem, solution, metrics, unfair advantage
Boxes are hypotheses until tested
Version per iteration — the model’s history
how_it_works: Draft the canvas, test each box, version per learning, align stakeholders on the current version.
t: The Lean Canvas and Business Model Canvas

title: The Ansoff Matrix
description: The Ansoff Matrix (1957) — the oldest growth framework still in use — maps growth strategies on two axes: products (existing/new) by markets (existing/new). The four quadrants: market penetration (existing/existing — sell more of what you have to whom you have — the lowest-risk growth), product development (new/existing — new offerings to current customers), market development (existing/new — current offerings to new segments or geographies), and diversification (new/new — the highest-risk quadrant, subdivided into related and unrelated). The operating use: the growth portfolio — the company’s bets mapped across quadrants with the risk budget explicit (most resources in penetration, measured bets in the riskier quadrants). The disciplines: the risk assessment per quadrant (diversification demands the strongest justification), the capability audit (new products/markets need new capabilities — named and built), and the quadrant review (the portfolio rebalanced yearly). The endurance: 65+ years because the question — what’s new, the product or the customer — never ages.
key_points: Four quadrants: penetration to diversification
Risk rises with newness of product and market
Portfolio the bets with explicit risk budget
Capability audit per new quadrant
how_it_works: Map growth bets to quadrants, assess risk, audit capabilities, allocate the risk budget, review yearly.

title: The BCG Growth-Share Matrix
description: The BCG matrix (1970s) — stars, cash cows, question marks, dogs — remains the portfolio framework executives reach for: businesses plotted by market growth (the industry’s attractiveness) and relative market share (the competitive position). The logic: cash cows fund stars (the portfolio’s internal capital market), question marks get invested or divested (the decisions the matrix forces), dogs get harvested or exited. The operating disciplines: define the market honestly (the share number depends on the market definition — the gaming of boundaries is the classic abuse), use forward growth (not last year’s), and make the resource decisions the matrix implies (the matrix without reallocation is wallpaper). The critiques: the matrix oversimplifies (share is not the only advantage; growth is not the only attractiveness), and it can justify neglecting the future (milking cows while stars starve). The modern use: the starting framework, enriched with capability and synergy analysis — the portfolio conversation’s common language.
key_points: Stars, cash cows, question marks, dogs
Cows fund stars: the internal capital market
Define markets honestly; use forward growth
Decisions implied must be made
core_principles: Fund the future from the present
how_it_works: Plot businesses honestly, allocate per the logic, decide the question marks, exit the dogs, review yearly.

title: GE-McKinsey Nine-Box Matrix
description: The GE-McKinsey nine-box — industry attractiveness by business strength, each on high/medium/low — refines BCG with multi-factor analysis: attractiveness scored on market size, growth, margins, competition, and risk; strength scored on share, brand, capabilities, and resources. The nine cells prescribe: invest/grow (high/high), selectively invest, harvest, or divest — the granularity BCG lacks. The operating use: the annual portfolio review — each business scored, debated, and assigned its strategic posture with the resource commitment to match. The disciplines: the scoring criteria defined before the scoring (the criteria debate is the strategy debate), the data honest (the business unit’s self-score needs the center’s verification), and the posture funded (the “invest” cell with no investment is the lie). The limitation: the matrix is a snapshot — the trajectory (where each business is moving) matters as much as the position. The best practice: score position and trajectory, and manage the movement.
key_points: Nine cells: attractiveness by strength, multi-factor
Prescriptions: invest, select, harvest, divest
Criteria defined before scoring; data verified
Position plus trajectory
how_it_works: Define criteria, score honestly, debate, assign postures, fund accordingly, track trajectory.

title: The Deming System of Profound Knowledge
description: W. Edwards Deming’s System of Profound Knowledge — the philosophy behind the quality revolution — has four lenses: appreciation for a system (the organization as interdependent components — optimizing parts suboptimizes wholes), knowledge of variation (common vs special causes — the statistical thinking that stops tampering), theory of knowledge (management as prediction — plans are theories, results test them), and psychology (people’s intrinsic motivation — the system must not destroy it). The 14 Points operationalize it: constancy of purpose, adopt the new philosophy, cease dependence on inspection, end price-only purchasing, improve constantly, institute training, institute leadership, drive out fear, break down barriers, eliminate slogans, eliminate quotas, remove barriers to pride of workmanship, institute education, take action. The power: the deepest management philosophy ever systematized — Japan’s postwar miracle ran on it. The demand: total — Deming insisted the system requires transformation, not tools. The modern relevance: every agile, lean, and quality practice traces to these roots.
key_points: Four lenses: systems, variation, knowledge, psychology
14 Points operationalize the philosophy
Japan’s miracle ran on it
Root of agile, lean, and quality practice
how_it_works: Study the four lenses, implement the 14 points, transform management thinking, sustain.
t: The Deming System of Profound Knowledge

title: The Toyota Way: The Two Pillars
description: The Toyota Way (documented 2001) — continuous improvement and respect for people, the two pillars holding the roof of the Toyota Production System. Continuous improvement: the challenge (ambitious goals), kaizen (everyone improving daily), and genchi genbutsu (go and see — reality over reports). Respect for people: respect (the dignity of every person — the prerequisite), and teamwork (the company’s success through people’s growth). The operating translation: the pillars are not posters — improvement runs through kaizen systems and andon authority; respect runs through lifetime employment philosophy, the safety to stop the line, and the investment in people’s development. The power: the culture that sustains the tools — TPS without the Way is mechanics without meaning, and mechanics without meaning decay. The lesson for adopters: the tools transfer easily; the pillars transfer only through leadership behavior — the Way is caught from leaders, not taught in classes. The test: do leaders go and see? If not, the Way is wallpaper.
key_points: Pillars: continuous improvement and respect for people
Improvement: challenge, kaizen, genchi genbutsu
Respect: dignity, teamwork, development
Caught from leaders, not taught in classes
how_it_works: Leaders model the pillars, install kaizen and andon systems, invest in people, go to the gemba.
t: The Toyota Way: The Two Pillars

title: The Netflix Culture Deck (Freedom and Responsibility)
description: Netflix’s culture deck (2009, “most important document ever to come out of Silicon Valley”) — freedom and responsibility as the operating system for creative talent. The principles: hire only fully-formed adults (the talent density bet — stunning colleagues), candor as the communication norm (radical honesty, kindly delivered), freedom with accountability (no vacation policy, no expense policy — “act in Netflix’s best interest”), context not control (leaders set context; people decide), and the keeper test (managers ask: would I fight to keep this person? — if no, fair severance now). The operating disciplines: the 360 feedbacks (the candor infrastructure), the compensation as top-of-market (the freedom to leave matched by the reason to stay), and the honest post-exit narratives. The power: the highest talent density in tech, sustained over decades. The demand: the system only works at extreme talent density — the freedom that empowers stars crushes strugglers. The lesson: culture as talent strategy — the deck is a recruiting document that filters.
key_points: Freedom and responsibility for fully-formed adults
No vacation/expense policy — act in best interest
Context not control; keeper test for talent
Works only at extreme talent density
how_it_works: Hire densely, grant freedom, demand candor, set context, test keepers, pay top of market.
t: The Netflix Culture Deck (Freedom and Responsibility)

title: Turnaround Frameworks: The First 100 Days
description: Corporate turnarounds follow a brutal, well-documented playbook — the first 100 days decide survival. The sequence: diagnose fast (the 30-day assessment — cash position, the real P&L, the talent audit, the customer truth — the facts before the plan), stabilize cash (the 13-week cash flow — the lifeline; stop the bleeding: cut non-essential spend, accelerate receivables, the triage), communicate honestly (employees, customers, lenders — the credibility that buys time), fix the commercial engine (the pricing, the key accounts, the sales focus — revenue before cost-cutting alone), restructure operations (the footprint, the headcount — the hard decisions with dignity), and rebuild the balance sheet (the debt renegotiation, the equity raise — the financial restructuring). The leadership: the turnaround CEO (the outsider with the mandate — the insider rarely survives the needed cuts), the war-room cadence (daily cash, weekly operations), and the stakeholder management (lenders as partners, not adversaries). The statistics: turnarounds attempted early succeed far more than late ones — the denial phase kills. The rule: act in weeks, not quarters.
key_points: Diagnose in 30 days; stabilize cash immediately
13-week cash flow as the lifeline
Communicate honestly to buy time
Early turnarounds succeed; denial kills
how_it_works: Assess fast, stabilize cash, communicate, fix commercial, restructure, rebuild balance sheet.

title: Good to Great: The Hedgehog and the Flywheel
description: Jim Collins’s Good to Great (2001) — the research on companies that leapt from good to great and sustained it — gave management two enduring frameworks. The Hedgehog Concept: the intersection of what you are deeply passionate about, what you can be the best in the world at, and what drives your economic engine — the three circles whose overlap defines the focused strategy (the fox knows many things; the hedgehog knows one big thing). The Flywheel: the compounding loop — disciplined people, disciplined thought, disciplined action — building momentum turn by turn, with no single miracle moment (the breakthrough is the flywheel’s accumulated turns, not the event). The supporting findings: Level 5 leadership (humility plus will), first who then what (the right people before the strategy), the culture of discipline (freedom within a framework of responsibility), technology as accelerator (not driver). The critiques: survivorship bias, the “great” companies’ later stumbles (Circuit City, Fannie Mae). The durable use: the hedgehog as the focus discipline, the flywheel as the patience discipline.
key_points: Hedgehog: passion, best-in-world, economic engine
Flywheel: disciplined momentum, no miracle moment
Level 5 leadership; first who then what
Technology accelerates; never drives
how_it_works: Find the hedgehog, get the right people, build disciplined momentum, let technology accelerate.
t: Good to Great: The Hedgehog and the Flywheel

title: The Innovator’s Dilemma Framework
description: Clayton Christensen’s Innovator’s Dilemma (1997) — the framework explaining why great companies fail at disruption. The mechanism: incumbents rationally serve their best customers with sustaining innovations (better products, higher margins), while disruptors enter at the low end with “good enough” offerings that incumbents ignore — until the disruptor’s trajectory meets the mainstream and the incumbent cannot respond (its processes, values, and profit formulas forbid the low-end fight). The prescriptions: the autonomous disruptive unit (separate organization with its own profit formula — the ambidextrous answer), the jobs-to-be-done lens (customers hire products for progress — compete on the job, not the product), and the discovery-driven planning (assumptions tested cheaply — the plan as hypothesis). The cases: steel minimills vs integrated mills, disk drives’ generations, the pattern repeating in industry after industry. The operating use: the disruption audit — where is the low end we are ignoring, and who is climbing toward us? The framework’s warning: the dilemma is rational — good management causes it, which is why it needs structural answers.
key_points: Rational incumbents ignore low-end disruptors until too late
Prescription: autonomous disruptive units
Jobs-to-be-done: compete on the customer’s job
Discovery-driven planning for uncertainty
how_it_works: Audit for low-end threats, charter autonomous units, plan by discovery, compete on jobs.

title: The McKinsey Three Horizons
description: The Three Horizons (Baghai, Coley, White — The Alchemy of Growth) — the time-horizon framework for managing the present and the future simultaneously. Horizon 1: the core businesses — defend and extend, the profits that fund everything (managed for efficiency). Horizon 2: the emerging businesses — the growth engines being built (managed for growth, funded deliberately). Horizon 3: the options — the experiments and seeds that may become H2 (managed for learning, cheap and many). The disciplines: resource allocation across horizons (the H1-only company eats its future; the H3-only company starves today — the balance is the strategy), different management per horizon (H1’s efficiency metrics would kill H3’s experiments), and the leadership attention split (the CEO’s calendar reflects the horizons — the future gets executive time, not just PowerPoints). The operating use: the annual strategy review allocates across horizons explicitly. The failure: the H2/H3 starvation — declared in strategy, unfunded in budgets. The rule: horizons get resources, metrics, and leadership — or they are fiction.
key_points: H1 core, H2 emerging, H3 options: managed differently
Allocate resources across horizons explicitly
Different metrics per horizon
CEO calendar reflects the future
how_it_works: Map initiatives to horizons, allocate resources and metrics per horizon, review the balance yearly.

title: Wardley Mapping
description: Wardley Mapping (Simon Wardley) — the strategy framework that maps components by value-chain position (y-axis: visible user needs at top, invisible infrastructure at bottom) and evolution (x-axis: genesis, custom, product, commodity — the left-to-right march of maturing components). The map reveals the strategic landscape: which components are commodities (buy/ outsource — the right side), which are differentiators (build — the left side), and where the evolution creates attacks (the innovate-leverage commoditization plays). The gameplay: the 40+ strategic plays (the “plays” — from vertical integration to open-sourcing as a weapon) chosen by landscape position. The operating use: the strategy workshop maps the business, debates the evolution, and chooses plays — the map makes strategic reasoning visible and arguable. The power: evolution-aware strategy — the component’s position on the x-axis predicts its future (today’s genesis is tomorrow’s commodity). The demand: the mapping skill — honest placement requires deep operational knowledge. The community: the open-source strategy movement’s flagship method.
key_points: Map by value chain (y) and evolution (x)
Commodities: buy; differentiators: build
Evolution predicts: genesis becomes commodity
40+ strategic plays by landscape position
how_it_works: Map components honestly, read the evolution, choose plays by position, execute, re-map.

title: The Cynefin Framework
description: Cynefin (Dave Snowden) — the sense-making framework for choosing management approaches by context domain. The five domains: simple (cause-effect obvious — sense, categorize, respond — best practice applies), complicated (cause-effect knowable with expertise — sense, analyze, respond — good practice, experts decide), complex (cause-effect only clear in retrospect — probe, sense, respond — emergent practice, safe-to-fail experiments), chaotic (no cause-effect — act, sense, respond — novel practice, stabilize first), and disorder (the domain of not knowing which domain — the dangerous default). The operating use: the leadership team places its challenges in domains and manages each accordingly — the complicated supply chain gets analysis; the complex market gets experiments; the chaotic crisis gets decisive action. The classic failure: managing complex challenges with simple-domain tools (the best-practice rollout into an emergent situation — the plan that cannot adapt). The power: the framework legitimizes different management per context — the end of one-size-fits-all. The practice: domain-shift awareness — challenges move domains, and management must move with them.
key_points: Five domains: simple, complicated, complex, chaotic, disorder
Each domain has its decision mode
Complex needs experiments, not best practice
Challenges shift domains; management must follow
how_it_works: Place challenges in domains, apply each domain’s mode, watch for domain shifts, adjust.

title: The Viable System Model (Beer)
description: Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model — the cybernetic theory of organizations that survive — defines the five systems any viable organization needs: System 1 (the operations — the value-creating units), System 2 (coordination — the anti-oscillation damping between units), System 3 (control — the operational management and resource bargaining), System 3* (audit — the sporadic monitoring channel), System 4 (intelligence — the outside-and-future scanning), and System 5 (policy — the identity and ethos). The model’s power: the diagnostic — organizational pathologies map to missing or weak systems (the company with no System 4 cannot see the future; the one with no System 2 oscillates). The variety engineering: management must match the environment’s complexity (Ashby’s law — only variety absorbs variety) through attenuation and amplification designed deliberately. The applications: the model has diagnosed governments, companies, and communities. The demand: the cybernetic thinking — the model rewards systems literacy. The insight that endures: viability is structural — the five systems present and recursing at every level.
key_points: Five systems: operations, coordination, control, intelligence, policy
Pathologies map to missing systems
Only variety absorbs variety (Ashby’s law)
Recursion: the pattern repeats at every level
how_it_works: Map the five systems, find the weak/missing, design variety engineering, recurse per level.

title: Choosing Frameworks: The Meta-Framework
description: With dozens of frameworks available, choosing becomes the meta-skill — and the method is situational. The selection questions: what is the actual problem (alignment? execution? quality? strategy? culture? turnaround?) — the problem names the framework family; what is the company’s size and stage (the startup’s EOS differs from the enterprise’s Hoshin) — the stage names the weight; what is the culture’s tolerance (command cultures reject holacracy; creative cultures reject Six Sigma) — the culture names the fit; and what is already installed (the new framework must integrate with or replace the old — the parallel-systems failure)? The combination rules: one primary OS (the coherent spine — EOS, Scaling Up, or equivalent), specialist frameworks per function (the quality team’s Six Sigma, the product team’s Scrum — integrated, not competing), and the review cycle (the framework audit — does each framework still serve?). The principle: frameworks serve the company; the company never serves the framework — the moment the framework becomes the point, it has failed.
key_points: Problem, stage, culture, installed base: the selection questions
One primary OS; specialist frameworks per function
Frameworks serve the company, never vice versa
Audit the framework set yearly
how_it_works: Diagnose needs, select situationally, install the spine, add specialists, audit yearly.

title: Framework Implementation: Making It Stick
description: Frameworks fail in implementation, not in design — the adoption disciplines decide. The sequence: the burning platform (the honest case for change — the why that survives the hard weeks), the coalition (the guiding team with credibility and authority), the pilot (one unit, measured — the proof before the rollout), the rollout (sequenced, supported, with the old system retired — parallel systems breed cynicism), and the sustainment (the audits, the coaching, the onboarding integration — the framework becomes “how we work”). The roles: the executive sponsor (the air cover), the implementer (the guide — internal or external), and the champions (the early adopters who sell peer-to-peer). The metrics: adoption (are the practices used?), fidelity (are they used rightly?), and outcomes (are results improving?). The timeline honesty: 6–12 months for team frameworks, 1–3 years for company OS — the shortcut attempts fail visibly. The rule: implement one framework well rather than three poorly — depth beats breadth in adoption.
key_points: Sequence: platform, coalition, pilot, rollout, sustainment
Roles: sponsor, implementer, champions
Metrics: adoption, fidelity, outcomes
One framework deeply beats three shallowly
how_it_works: Build the case, form the coalition, pilot measured, roll out sequenced, sustain via audits and onboarding.
